127.title: A chapter a day
127.hook: most Bible-reading habits are small: one chapter, same time, every day
127.howItsDone: Some Christians read a chapter or a set passage of the Bible every day, often with a reading plan, a daily devotional or the church's lectionary, at a regular time such as early morning or before bed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two testaments, and your line: the story began long before. Today, how people actually keep reading.

January first. A fresh start, and a big resolution: this is the year I read the whole Bible, cover to cover. You start at Genesis. Creation, the flood, Abraham, Joseph: it moves. Exodus: plagues, the sea splitting. Then you reach Leviticus, chapter after chapter of rules for sacrifices, offerings and purity, and somewhere in there the bookmark stops moving. There's an older way in, and it isn't a grand plan. It's small. One chapter. Same time. Same chair. Every day.
screen: `THIS IS THE YEAR.` → `ON TO LEVITICUS.` → `THE BOOKMARK STOPS.`

segments.voice: The idea is old. In the book of Acts, the people of a town called Berea are praised because they "searched the scriptures daily." Not in one heroic weekend. God tells Joshua, "thou shalt meditate therein day and night." A little, often. A chapter of a Gospel takes a few minutes to read, about as long as this lesson. Here's a surprise: chapter numbers aren't part of the original text. The biblical writers didn't use them. Chapter divisions were added many centuries later, and verse numbers later still. They're handles, and Christians have built all kinds of plans on them. A Scottish minister, Robert Murray M'Cheyne, made a plan to take his congregation through the Bible in a year. The Book of Common Prayer takes Anglicans through the whole book of Psalms every month. Catholics hear scripture in a set cycle of readings at Mass, and some Protestants use reading plans on their phones. If you're starting from nothing, a common piece of advice is: don't start at Genesis. Start with a Gospel. Mark has sixteen chapters: sixteen days, and you've read a whole account of the life of Jesus. Missed a day? The plan doesn't care. You pick it up where you left off.
screen: `THEY SEARCHED THE SCRIPTURES DAILY.` · `A LITTLE, OFTEN.` · `CHAPTERS CAME LATER.` · `START WITH MARK.`

segments.voice: Picture your ordinary day and find a few minutes that are already yours, morning coffee, the bus, lunch, right before bed, and a place to match: a chair, a corner, a seat on the train. See yourself there with a Bible, or an app, open to Mark, chapter one. If you pray, offer that time to God before it starts; if you don't, simply decide it's yours.
Capitulum, Latin for a little head, a heading, the root of the word chapter: a small, steady habit, one chapter at a time.
Your line: small and daily wins. Mark chapter one is a good door. That's day one hundred twenty-seven.

screen: `DAY 127 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A LAMP FOR MY FEET (PSALM 119:105)`

128.title: A lamp for my feet (Psalm 119:105)
128.hook: people memorize a verse to carry it in the dark
128.howItsDone: Some Christians memorize Bible verses, often starting in childhood Sunday school, and repeat them in hard moments.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a chapter a day, capitulum, and your line: small and daily wins. Today, something even smaller: one verse, carried.

Ever walked a dark path at night with only your phone's flashlight? A camping trip, a power cut, a country road. The light doesn't show you the whole way. It shows the next two steps: a root, a puddle, the edge of the path. And that turns out to be enough. You keep walking, two steps at a time. Now an older kind of light: a little clay oil lamp, small enough to hold in your palm, with a wick and a tiny flame. In ancient Israel, people carried lamps like that at night. It didn't light up the road ahead. It lit your feet. Today's word comes from someone who knew that kind of light.
screen: `A PHONE FLASHLIGHT ON A DARK PATH.` → `THE NEXT TWO STEPS.` → `A CLAY LAMP IN YOUR PALM.`

segments.voice: Here it is, from Psalm 119, in the King James Bible: "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path." Not a floodlight. Not a map of the next ten years. Enough light for the next step. That's the psalm's picture of God's word: not seeing everything, but not walking blind. Psalm 119, a hundred and seventy-six verses long, is built like a puzzle. In Hebrew it's an alphabet poem: twenty-two sections, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet, and in each section all eight verses begin with that letter. Our verse opens the section for the letter nun, and the Hebrew word for lamp, ner, starts with it. Verse after verse names God's word in some form: law, statutes, precepts, commandments. The poet says it outright: "O how love I thy law!" Earlier in the same psalm is a line that explains why people memorize verses at all: "Thy word have I hid in mine heart." Hid, as in stored away. Jews and Christians both learn verses by heart. A verse learned by heart goes where a book can't: into a hospital bed, a prison cell, a sleepless night, a moment with no phone and no light. It's a lamp you don't have to find in the dark.
screen: `NOT A FLOODLIGHT: THE NEXT STEP.` · `176 VERSES, AN ALPHABET POEM.` · `THY WORD HAVE I HID IN MINE HEART.` · `A LAMP YOU CARRY INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Say the first half slowly, thy word is a lamp unto my feet, then the second, and a light unto my path, a few times each, letting each phrase land on a breath. Then put them together and keep repeating the whole verse quietly, without rushing. If you pray, make it a prayer; if you don't, just let it settle in.
screen: `THY WORD IS A LAMP UNTO MY FEET, AND A LIGHT UNTO MY PATH.`

segments.voice: Ner, the Hebrew word for lamp, opening the section of Psalm 119 for the letter nun: enough light for the next step.
Your line: a lamp unto my feet. Learned by heart, it goes wherever you go. Until tomorrow.

129.title: Reading slowly
129.hook: reading for information and reading for formation are different speeds
129.howItsDone: Some Christians read scripture slowly, often aloud or under their breath, repeating a phrase and pausing on a word; monks and nuns practice this as lectio divina, and some Protestants read a single verse slowly in a morning quiet time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ner, a lamp for my feet, and your line: a lamp unto my feet. Today, the speed you read at.

The terms and conditions on a new app: scroll, scroll, agree. Now a different page: a letter in a drawer, in the handwriting of someone who has died, found years later. That one gets read slowly. A pause at a phrase. A second reading. One sentence, ten times over, until the voice comes back. Same eyes, same alphabet, completely different reading. Headlines, feeds and emails tend to get the first speed: skimming for what's needed. Some Christian teachers say the Bible is meant to be read, at least sometimes, at the second.
screen: `TERMS AND CONDITIONS: SCROLL, AGREE.` → `A LETTER FOUND IN A DRAWER.` → `TWO SPEEDS OF READING.`

segments.voice: Some Christian writers call the two speeds reading for information and reading for formation. The first asks: what does this say? The second asks: what is this doing to me? Both matter, they say: the first tells you what's there, and the second is where the words start to shape a life. The Bible itself describes the slow kind. The first psalm, the one from three days ago, praises the person whose "delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night." That word meditate, in Hebrew hagah, doesn't mean sitting silent with an empty mind. It means to murmur, to mutter under your breath. Isaiah uses the same word for a lion growling over its prey. So the picture is someone going over the words out loud, again and again, low and slow, like a lion that won't let go. Augustine, in his Confessions, describes watching the bishop Ambrose read with his eyes moving and his voice silent, and wondering why. Some medieval monks called slow reading rumination: chewing on the words the way a cow chews the cud. You met their method on day one hundred one, lectio divina: read, notice a word, ponder, rest. Christians from different churches read this way in some form: monks and nuns, some Protestants with a single verse in a morning quiet time, people who imagine themselves into a Gospel scene. At full speed, the words pass through you. Slowed down, one word can hold you for a whole minute.
screen: `INFORMATION, THEN FORMATION.` · `HAGAH: TO MURMUR.` · `A LION THAT WON'T LET GO.` · `ONE WORD CAN HOLD YOU.`

segments.voice: If you have a Bible, open to Psalm 23 and take the first five verses; if not, its first line: "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want." Read it once at normal speed, then again twice as slowly, murmuring under your breath, and when one word catches you, stop there and say it again. If you pray, let that word become your prayer; if you don't, just stay with it.
screen: `THE LORD IS MY SHEPHERD; I SHALL NOT WANT.`

segments.voice: Reading slowly. Reading for formation, not only information: murmuring the words until one stops you. Today's word.
Your line: slow down to hear. Information first, then formation. That's one hundred twenty-nine days.

130.title: Tyndale's plow
130.hook: Tyndale died so a ploughboy could read the Bible in English; many translations followed, KJV and Douay-Rheims among them
130.howItsDone: Christians read the Bible in many translations; Protestants often use versions descended from Tyndale and the King James, Catholics use approved Catholic translations descended from the Douay-Rheims tradition, and Bible societies of many churches work to translate it into every language.

segments.voice: Yesterday, reading slowly, and your line: slow down to hear. Today, the last of ten days on sabbath and scripture: how those words reached English.

England, the 1520s. A young scholar named William Tyndale, who reads Greek and Hebrew, gets into an argument with a churchman. The story goes that Tyndale told him, if God spared his life, he'd see to it that a boy who drives the plow would know more of the scriptures than he did. Translating the Bible into English without church permission was forbidden, so Tyndale left England for good. In Germany, in 1526, he printed a New Testament in English, small enough to hide. Copies were smuggled across the sea in bales of cloth, and many were burned. Nine years later, he was betrayed and arrested in Antwerp, and in 1536, near Brussels, he was strangled and his body burned. The story is that he died praying that God would open the king of England's eyes.
screen: `A BOY WHO DRIVES THE PLOW.` → `SMUGGLED IN BALES OF CLOTH.` → `ARRESTED, STRANGLED, BURNED.`

segments.voice: Every Bible in English is a carrying-across, from Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek. Before Tyndale, followers of John Wycliffe had copied English Bibles by hand, translated from Latin. Tyndale went back to the original languages, and he had an ear. He gave English words and phrases it still uses: Passover. Scapegoat. Let there be light. The salt of the earth. The King James Bible of 1611 leaned heavily on him; scholars estimate most of its New Testament is his. So when you've heard the King James quoted on this path, you've often been hearing Tyndale. English Catholics made their own translation too, in exile in France, from the Latin: the Rheims New Testament in 1582 and the Douai Old Testament decades later. That's the Douay-Rheims, the Catholic Bible in English for centuries. It was a violent age on every side. Protestants and Catholics were both put to death for their faith. Thomas More, who wrote fiercely against Tyndale, was himself executed by Henry the Eighth a year before Tyndale died. Christians of every church remember their own martyrs from that time. What nearly all Christians share now is the conviction that anyone should be able to read the Bible in their own language. Today it has been translated in full into hundreds of languages, and in part into thousands more. Every one cost someone years; some cost a life.
screen: `TRANSLATION: CARRIED ACROSS.` · `PASSOVER, SCAPEGOAT, LET THERE BE LIGHT.` · `KING JAMES AND DOUAY-RHEIMS.` · `A VIOLENT AGE ON EVERY SIDE.`

segments.voice: Remember who taught you to read: a parent with a picture book, a first-grade teacher, an older sibling, a librarian, someone who pointed at letters until they became words. See their face if you can, and think what that one gift has opened for you since. If you pray, give thanks for them by name; if you don't, just feel grateful.
Translation. From the Latin for carried across. The work that brought the Bible from Hebrew and Greek into English, at great cost.
Your line: words cost someone something. Tomorrow, a whole new stretch begins: giving and singing.

131.title: The tithe (Malachi 3:10)
131.hook: many Christians give a tenth; others give differently, but most give regularly
131.howItsDone: Christians give to their church and to the poor in different ways; some tithe ten percent of their income, while others give a proportion they decide themselves, often through a weekly offering or a regular automatic gift.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tyndale and translation, and your line: words cost someone something. That closed sabbath and scripture. Now a new stretch: giving and singing.

Payday. The money lands in your account, and within minutes it's already spoken for: rent, groceries, the phone bill, the car, the thing you promised your kid. Whatever's left at the end of the month is what's left. Now go back to Genesis, to Abram, the man who'll become Abraham. He's just come back from a battle, and a mysterious priest-king named Melchizedek comes out to meet him with bread and wine, and blesses him. Abram's response fits in one line. In the King James words: "And he gave him tithes of all." A tenth of everything.
screen: `PAYDAY, ALREADY SPOKEN FOR.` → `ABRAM AND MELCHIZEDEK.` → `TITHES OF ALL.`

segments.voice: Tithe is an old English word meaning a tenth. In the Hebrew scriptures, tithes of grain, wine, oil and flocks supported the priests and Levites who served at the sanctuary, and some went to the poor: the widow, the orphan and the stranger. Worship and welfare in one. Then the prophet Malachi, speaking to people who had held back their tithes: "Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing." Christians today read that verse in different ways. Some churches, often evangelical or Pentecostal, teach tithing as a standard: a tenth of income, given to the local church. Others, Catholic and Orthodox among them, teach generous, regular giving without a fixed number, and point to Paul: "every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." Some preachers read Malachi as a promise that giving will make you rich; other Christians firmly reject that reading. A thread through these views is firstfruits. Proverbs says, "Honour the LORD with thy substance, and with the firstfruits of all thine increase." The first of the harvest, not the leftovers. For those who teach it, the point isn't the math. It's the order. Giving that comes first shapes everything after it. Giving that waits for the leftovers often finds none.
screen: `TITHE: A TENTH.` · `WORSHIP AND WELFARE IN ONE.` · `A TENTH, OR A CHEERFUL GIVER.` · `FIRSTFRUITS, NOT LEFTOVERS.`

segments.voice: Think of something you care about, a church, a food bank, a neighbor, a cause, and one small, regular gift you could give it: money in an amount so small it doesn't scare you, an hour a month, or a skill. Don't decide the whole plan, only the first gift and when it happens. If you pray, offer it to God before it leaves your hands; if you don't, simply choose it freely.
Tithe. A tenth: the old practice of giving the first part of what you have to God and to those in need. Today's word.
Your line: give first, not last. The gift itself can be small. That's day one hundred thirty-one.

132.title: Pastors and money
132.hook: a preacher's sneakers go viral; the New Testament has more to say about church money than people expect
132.howItsDone: Many churches publish annual budgets, have an elected board or council set clergy pay, and use outside audits; members are generally free to ask how gifts are spent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tithe, and your line: give first, not last. Today, the question that comes right after giving: where does it go?

A photo goes around online. A preacher on a big stage, mid-sermon, arms raised. Someone has circled his sneakers in red and added a price: a few thousand dollars. Underneath, the comments pile up. Is this where my tithe goes? There are whole accounts built around pictures like that, and some people quietly stop giving because of them. It's a fair question, and an old one. The first Christians asked it too, and the New Testament answers it more directly than people expect. Today's word is an old one for money made the wrong way.
screen: `THE CIRCLED SNEAKERS.` → `IS THIS WHERE MY TITHE GOES?` → `A FAIR, OLD QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Lucre. It means gain or profit, from the Latin lucrum, and the King James Bible usually puts a word in front of it: filthy lucre. Here's a letter written to church leaders, in that translation: "Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind." The Greek behind it means for shameful gain. So the warning about leaders in it for the money isn't a modern cynic's idea. It's in the Bible. Now the other side. Paul says plainly that "they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel." Paying a pastor isn't a scandal, and some pastors work a second job so a small church can afford them. Paul himself often worked with his hands, making tents, so no one could say he preached for money. Then the part for anyone who has wondered where their gift goes. Paul was carrying a large collection from the churches to the poor in Jerusalem, and he refused to handle it alone. Others, chosen by the churches, traveled with it. His reason, in the King James words: "Providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men." Honest before God, and visible to everyone else. That's still the shape many churches aim for: open books, a board that sets the pastor's pay, outside checks. Some publish their budgets for anyone to read. Asking where the money goes isn't a lack of faith. Paul expected the question.
screen: `LUCRE: GAIN, FROM LATIN LUCRUM.` · `NOT FOR FILTHY LUCRE.` · `THE WORKER IS PAID.` · `HONEST IN THE SIGHT OF ALL.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a place you give to, or once did, or might, a church, a charity, a friend's fundraiser, and notice what you know about where the money goes, and what you don't. No suspicion needed, and no guilt: just honest eyes, the kind Paul asked for. If you pray, pray for the people who handle gifts, that they'd be faithful; if you don't, simply hold the question kindly.
Lucre. Gain or profit, from the Latin lucrum. Church leaders are told to serve not for filthy lucre. Today's word.
Your line: open books, open hands. Giving freely and asking where it goes belong together. Day one hundred thirty-two.

133.title: Give in secret (Matthew 6:1–4)
133.hook: don't let your left hand know what your right hand is doing
133.howItsDone: Many Christians give to the poor quietly, through unsigned gifts, anonymous envelopes or church funds that keep donors' names private, taking Jesus's words about secret giving as their guide.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pastors and money, lucre, and your line: open books, open hands. Open books are for the church. Today, the giver's side, which Jesus wanted closed.

A coffee paid for, for the stranger behind you in line. Trash picked up in the stairwell. A small kindness nobody saw. And then, sometimes, a tiny wish that someone had: that it might come up in conversation, or that the person might turn around in time to see who it was. It's an old and very human wish, and Jesus, in the middle of the Sermon on the Mount, puts his finger right on it. He describes someone giving to the poor with a trumpet blowing in front of them.
screen: `A KINDNESS NOBODY SAW.` → `A TINY WISH TO BE SEEN.` → `A TRUMPET IN FRONT OF THE GIFT.`

segments.voice: Alms is an old English word for gifts to the poor. It comes, through Latin, from the Greek eleēmosynē, which grows out of eleos, mercy. So alms are mercy you can hold in your hand. The same root sits in the old church cry Kyrie eleison: Lord, have mercy. In Matthew chapter six, Jesus doesn't say whether to give. He takes that for granted, and talks about how. In the King James words: "when thou doest thine alms, do not sound a trumpet before thee, as the hypocrites do." Nobody is sure anyone literally blew a trumpet. Some readers think it's a picture, a joke even, like don't toot your own horn. Others connect it to the trumpet-shaped offering boxes said to stand in the Temple. Either way, the point lands: people who give for applause get the applause, and that's all they get. Then the strangest line: "let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth." You can't hide something from your own hand. That's the point: a gift so quiet that even you barely make a story of it. "That thine alms may be in secret: and thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly." Christians have found plenty of quiet ways: the anonymous envelope, the unsigned check, groceries left on a porch. Jews have a long tradition here too; the medieval teacher Maimonides ranked a gift where giver and receiver don't know each other near the very top. The idea underneath is freeing. A secret gift can't buy anything back: no thanks, no reputation, no story to tell.
